passages.source_text: καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἀδύνατα λέγεις· καὶ γὰρ κατ’ ὀλίγον γινόμενον αὐτὸν ὡς ἐχθρὸν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ προαιρέσει ἀνελεῖν ἠδύνατο. καὶ προγινώσκων γίνεσθαι αὐτὸν οὐ καλόν, οὐ συνεχώρει, εἰ μὴ πρὸς τὸ αὐτῷ χρήσιμον γινόμενον ἠπίστατο καὶ τέλειος ἐξαίφνης ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ γενέσθαι οὐχ οἷός τε ἦν· ἑαυτὸν γὰρ ὁ μήπω ὢν πλάττειν οὐκ ἐδύνατο οὔτε ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων γενέσθαι τί οὐσίαν ἔχει δύναται καὶ γεννητὸν ὑπάρχον τῷ ἀεὶ ἰσοδυναμεῖν οὐκ ὀρθῶς ἂν εἴποι τις. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Μήτι οὖν τῶν· πρὸς τί ἐστι καὶ οὕτως πονηρόν ἐστι; κακὸν μὲν ὂν ὡς ὕδωρ πυρί, ἀγαθὸν δὲ τῇ ἀκαίρως διψώσῃ γῇ· ὥσπερ γε καὶ σίδηρος εἰς μὲν γεωργίαν καλός, εἰς δὲ φόνους κακός — καὶ ἡ ἐπιθυμία δὲ εἰς μὲν γάμους οὐ κακή, εἰς δὲ μοιχείαν χαλεπή — ὡς καὶ τὸ φονεῦσαι κακόν, ἀλλὰ τῷ φονεύσαντι πρὸς ὃ βεβούλευται καλόν — καὶ ἡ πλεονεξία κακόν, ἀλλὰ τῷ πλεονεκτοῦντι ἡδὺ — καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα τυγχάνει, τοῦτον περιέχει τὸν τρόπον. τούτῳ δὲ τῷ λόγῳ οὔτε τὸ κακὸν κακόν ἐστιν οὔτε τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἀγαθὸν τυγχάνει· ἑκάτερον γὰρ τὸ ἕτερον ἐργάζεται. μήτιγε τὸ δοκοῦν κακῶς γίνεσθαι εὐφραίνει μὲν τὸν ποιοῦντα, κολάζει δὲ τὸν πάσχοντα; καὶ εἰ ἄδικον δοκεῖ τὸ ἑαυτὸν ἀγαπήσαντα. εὐφραίνειν ὡς δυνατόν ἐστι· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο χαλεπὰ πείσεσθαι ὑπὸ δικαίου δικαστοῦ περὶ τοῦ ἑαυτὸν ἠγαπηκέναι, τίνι οὐκ ἄδικον φαίνεται;

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἑαυτὸν χρὴ κολάζειν τότε τῇ ἐγκρατείᾳ, ὅταν ἡ ἐπιθυμία πρὸς ἑτέρου βλάβην ὁρμῆσαι θέλῃ, εἰδότα ὅτι ὁ πονηρὸς τοὺς μὲν κακοὺς ἀνελεῖν δύναται, ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς τὴν κατ’ αὐτῶν εἰληφὼς ἐξουσίαν· καὶ οὕτω τοῦτο κακὸν τοῖς κακὰ πράξασιν, ἀλλὰ τὸ μετὰ τὴν ἀναίρεσιν τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν κολαζομένας διαμένειν, τοῦτο ὄντως εἶναι χαλεπὸν δικαίως τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον ὀρθῶς ἔχειν εἰπόντος· οὗ εἵνεκεν παραιτεῖσθαι χρὴ (ὡς ἔφην) βραχείας χάριν ἡδονῆς ἄλλον ἀδικεῖν πρὸς τὸ μὴ αὐτόν τινα ὀλίγης χάριν ἡδονῆς ἀιδίῳ περιβαλεῖν κολάσει. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Μήτι οὖν οὐκ ἔστι τῇ φύσει πονηρὸν ἢ ἀγαθόν, ἀλλὰ νόμῳ διαφέρει καὶ ἔθει ..̓̀. παρὰ Πέρσαις ἴδιον τὸ γαμεῖν μητέρας, ἀδελφάς, θυγατέρας, ἄλλοις δὲ ὥσπερ χαλεπώτ[ατον ἀπη]γόρευται. ὅθεν τῶν κακῶν μὴ ὡρισμένων πᾶσι τὴν ἐκ θεοῦ κρίσιν προσδοκᾶν οὐκ ἔστι. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Οὐ δύνασαι τοῦτο συστῆσαι· πᾶσι γὰρ φαίνεται ὅτι τὸ μητράσι μίγνυσθαι μυσαρόν, κἂν Πέρσαι, μόριον ὑπάρχοντες τοῦ παντός, ὑπὸ κακοῦ ἔθους τῆς μυσαρᾶς αὐτῶν πράξεως τὸ ἄνομον μὴ ἀντιλαμβάνωνται. ὡς καὶ Βρεττανοὶ ἐμφανῶς ἐπὶ πάντων κοινωνοῦσι καὶ οὐκ αἰδοῦνται — καὶ ἄλλοι σάρκας ἀνθρώπων ἐσθίουσι καὶ οὐ μυσάττονται, καὶ ἕτεροι κυνῶν — καὶ ἄλλοι ἄρρητα πράσσουσιν. οὕτως οὐ χρὴ αἰσθήσει ὑπὸ ἔθους τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ἐκτραπείσῃ τὰς κρίσεις ποιεῖσθαι. καὶ γὰρ τὸ φονευθῆναι κακόν ἐστι, κἂν μὴ πάντες λέγωσιν ὅτι μηδεὶς αὐτοπαθεῖν θέλει, καὶ κλοπῇ οὐδεὶς ἐπὶ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ κολάσει ἥδεται. κἂν οὖν ἑνὸς οὐδήποτε ὁμολογουμένου εἶναι ἁμαρτήματα, ἐξ ἀνάγκης καὶ τρίτην κρίσιν πρὸς τὰ ἁμαρτήματα ὀρθῶς ἔστι προσδοκᾶν. ταῦτα τοῦ Πέτρου εἰπόντος ὁ Σίμων ἀπεκρίνατο Οὕτως σοι δοκεῖ τὰ κατὰ τὸν πονηρὸν εἶναι, εἰπέ μοι.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Μεμνήμεθα τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ διδασκάλου ὡς ἐντελλόμενος εἶπεν ἡμῖν „τὰ μυστήρια ἐμοὶ καὶ τοῖς υἱοῖς τοῦ οἴκου μου φυλάξατε“· διὸ καὶ „τοῖς αὐτοῦ μαθηταῖς κατ’ ἰδίαν ἐπέλυε“ τῆς τῶν οὐρανῶν βασιλείας τὰ μυστήρια. σοὶ δέ, πολεμοῦντι ἡμᾶς καὶ μηδὲν ἕτερον διασκοποῦντι ἢ τὰ ἡμέτερα .... (εἴτε ἀληθῆ ὄντα εἴτε ψευδῆ) τὰ ἀπόρρητα λέγειν ἀσεβεῖν ἐστίν. ἀλλ’ ἵνα μὴ δόξωσί τινες τῶν παρεστώτων ὅτι ἀδυνατῶν πρὸς τὰ ὑπὸ σοῦ ῥηθέντα ἀποκρίνασθαι προφάσεως διαμηχανῶμαι, ἐρῶ πρότερον πυνθανόμενός σου εἰ τὸ μὴ ἀλγεῖν ἦν, τί ἂν ἔτι ἦν ὁ πονηρός; καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Οὐδέν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἀρά γε τὸ πονηρὸν τὸ ἀλγεῖν ἐστὶ καὶ τὸ θανεῖν; καὶ ὁ Σίμων Φαίνεται. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Οὐκ ἄρα ὑπάρχει τὸ πονηρὸν ἀεί, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ μὴν ὑπάρξαι δύναται· τὸ γὰρ ἀλγῆσαι καὶ θανεῖν τῶν συμβαινόντων ἐστίν, ὧν οὐδέτερόν ἐστι παρούσης εὐσθενείας. τί γὰρ ἔστιν ἀλγεῖν ἤ τι ἀναρμοστεῖν; τί δὲ θάνατος ἢ χωρισμὸς ψυχῆς ἀπὸ σώματος; οὔτ’ οὖν ἁρμονίας οὔσης τὸ ἀλγεῖν ἔστι· τὸ γὰρ θανεῖν οὐδὲ ὅλως τῶν ὑπαρκτῶν ἐστίν, ὅτι θάνατος οὐδέν ἐστιν (ὡς ἔφην) ἢ χωρισμὸς ψυχῆς ἀπὸ σώματος, οὗ συμβάντος τὸ μὲν σῶμα φύσει ἀναίσθητον ὂν λύεται, ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ αἰσθητὴ οὖσα ζῶσα ὑπάρχει — ὅθεν ἁρμονίας οὔσης οὐκ ἀλγεῖν ἔστιν, οὐκ ἀποθανεῖν, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ μὴν βοτάναι θανάσιμοι, οὐχ ἑρπετὰ ἰοβόλα οὐδὲ ἄλλο τι τοιοῦτον, οὗ τὸ τέλος θάνατος. ὅθεν ἀθανασίας ἐπικρατούσης εὐλόγως πάντα γεγονότα φανήσεται. ὅπερ καὶ οὕτως ἔσται, ὁπόταν δικαιοσύνης αἰτίᾳ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἀθάνατος γένηται τῆς τοῦ χριστοῦ εἰρηνικῆς ἐπικρατούσης βασιλείας ὅτε αὐτοῦ καὶ ἡ κρᾶσις εὔκρατός ἐστιν, ἵνα μὴ ὀξείας........ ὁρμάς, ἔτι τε καὶ γνῶσις ἄπταιστος, ἵνα μή τι τῶν κακῶν ὡς ἀγαθὸν π....... τε ἀλγῶν ἔσται, ἵνα μὴ θνητὸς ᾖ.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text:
Peter said, “You are saying impossible things. For even while he was coming into being little by little, he could have chosen to destroy him as an enemy himself. And, knowing beforehand that he would become not good, he would not have allowed it unless he knew that his coming into being would serve his own use. Nor was he capable of suddenly coming into being fully developed by himself, for someone who did not yet exist could not fashion himself. Nor can anything that has substance come into being out of what does not exist. And one could not rightly say that something that has come into being is equal in power to what always exists.”

Simon said, “Is it perhaps, then, one of the things that are relative, and is it evil in this way? It is bad, for example, as water is to fire, but good for ground that is untimely thirsty. Iron likewise is good for farming but bad for murders; desire, too, is not bad for marriage but is harmful for adultery. So also killing is bad, but good for the killer in relation to what he has planned. And greed is bad, but pleasant for the greedy person. Everything of this sort follows this pattern. By this argument, neither is evil evil, nor is good good, for each produces the other. Does not what seems to be done evilly bring delight to the doer but punishment to the sufferer? And if it seems unjust for someone who has loved himself to enjoy himself as much as possible, and because of this to suffer grievously at the hands of a righteous judge for having loved himself, to whom does it not appear unjust?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἐχθρὸν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ προαιρέσει ἀνελεῖν ἠδύνατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: he could have chosen to destroy him as an enemy himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: God remains the understood subject of ἠδύνατο. προαιρέσει specifies choice, and ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ is represented reflexively as personal agency, “himself.” Another attachment is “as an enemy brought into being by him”; the Greek arrangement does not make the attachment entirely unambiguous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων γενέσθαι τί οὐσίαν ἔχει δύναται
lexical_decisions.chosen: Nor can anything that has substance come into being out of what does not exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied Greek has finite ἔχει (“it has”) beside δύναται (“can”), not a participle meaning “having” and not an expressed relative pronoun. I understand οὐσίαν ἔχει as a loose or parenthetic predication about the indefinite τί, “anything”: “nor can anything—it has substance—come into being out of what does not exist.” The main text integrates that predication into readable attributive English, “anything that has substance,” because the argument is discussing whether an existing being could arise from nonexistence. This is an English syntactic unpacking, not a change of the Greek to ἔχον or the insertion of a relative pronoun. A material alternative is to retain the parenthetic linkage, “Nor can anything—it has substance—come into being out of what does not exist.” That reading can assert substance of the particular posited being rather than limit the denial to a class of things that have substance. The Greek does not uniquely settle this linkage or scope. The negation and the supplied finite ἔχει are retained; the sentence is not harmonized with earlier competing claims about creation from nonexistence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: one of the things that are relative
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρός τι is the category of what is relative to something else; the supplied punctuation does not require a separate English clause. The following examples explicitly compare different effects on different recipients.
ἀκαίρως marks untimeliness or being out of season. “Ground thirsty at the wrong time” is an alternative; the adverb is not dropped as though the text merely said dry ground.
χαλεπή characterizes desire as difficult, harsh, or harmful in its adulterous use. “Troublesome” is possible but could understate the evaluative contrast.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ εἰ ἄδικον δοκεῖ τὸ ἑαυτὸν ἀγαπήσαντα. εὐφραίνειν ὡς δυνατόν ἐστι· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο χαλεπὰ πείσεσθαι ὑπὸ δικαίου δικαστοῦ περὶ τοῦ ἑαυτὸν ἠγαπηκέναι, τίνι οὐκ ἄδικον φαίνεται;
source_issues.issue: The wording has a difficult scope for the first “unjust”: the articular infinitive and subsequent infinitive can gather the self-pleasuring and its punishment into a single stated situation. The main text retains both occurrences of “unjust” and the positive “loved himself” rather than supplying a missing negation or turning the opening adjective into “just.” Another reading would take the initial description of injustice as Simon’s concession before his challenge about punishment. The supplied punctuation after ἀγαπήσαντα is not treated as a completed sentence.

passages.text:
Peter said, “One must discipline oneself through self-control whenever desire wants to rush toward another person’s harm, knowing that the evil one can destroy evil people, having received authority against them from the beginning. And so this is evil for those who have done evil. But that their souls remain under punishment after their destruction—this is indeed grievous, with someone rightly saying that the previously wrongly defined [one] is correct. For this reason, as I said, one must refuse to wrong someone else for the sake of a brief pleasure, so as not to bring oneself into everlasting punishment for the sake of a little pleasure.”

Simon said, “Is it perhaps, then, that there is nothing evil or good by nature, but the difference is a matter of law and custom ..̓̀.? Among Persians, marrying mothers, sisters, and daughters is a distinctive practice, whereas among others it is forbidden as something most grievous. Thus, since evils have not been defined for everyone, one cannot expect judgment from God.”

Peter said, “You cannot establish this. For it is apparent to everyone that having intercourse with mothers is abhorrent, even if Persians, who are one part of the whole, do not recognize the lawlessness of their abhorrent practice because of bad custom. So too Britons openly share with one another in front of everyone and feel no shame. Others eat human flesh and do not feel disgust, and others eat dogs’ flesh; still others do things that cannot be spoken of. Thus one must not make judgments by a perception that custom has diverted from what is natural. For being murdered is evil, even if not everyone says that no one wants to experience it himself; and no one takes pleasure in theft when it means his own punishment. So even if in any one case it is acknowledged that there are sins, we must necessarily and rightly also expect a third judgment concerning those sins.”

After Peter said this, Simon replied, “Is this how matters concerning the evil one seem to you? Tell me.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative specifies the means of disciplining oneself. “Restraint” is another direct rendering.
ἀΐδιος explicitly conveys everlasting or eternal duration; the wording does not substitute “age-long,” and κολάσει is rendered punishment without making an additional claim about its purpose.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἴδιον τὸ γαμεῖν μητέρας, ἀδελφάς, θυγατέρας
lexical_decisions.chosen: marrying mothers, sisters, and daughters is a distinctive practice
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἴδιον means peculiar or distinctive to the people named. The main text translates the ancient speaker’s assertion without independently endorsing the historical ethnographic claim or adding erotic description.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς καὶ Βρεττανοὶ ἐμφανῶς ἐπὶ πάντων κοινωνοῦσι
lexical_decisions.chosen: So too Britons openly share with one another in front of everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: κοινωνοῦσι means participate or share; an object such as wives or sexual partners is not explicitly stated. The contextual implication is left to the reader rather than supplied as surviving source wording.
The preceding σάρκας…ἐσθίουσι supplies the ellipsis; κυνῶν is the genitive “of dogs.”
The selected source expressly has τρίτην, “third.” No change to “future judgment” or other conjectural reading is made, although the enumeration is not explained in this passage.

source_issues.source_quote: τοῦτο ὄντως εἶναι χαλεπὸν δικαίως τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον ὀρθῶς ἔχειν εἰπόντος
source_issues.issue: The construction can be read as a genitive absolute, εἰπόντος, with its speaker unexpressed: “with someone rightly saying.” δικαίως qualifies the saying; the accusative masculine τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον is then the subject of the reported infinitive ὀρθῶς ἔχειν, “is correct” or “is in a right condition.” This analysis accounts for the surviving forms without emending the Greek or identifying an unexpressed speaker. The main text retains the unspecified masculine referent as “[one].” It could denote a person or being previously wrongly characterized; alternatively, with λόγον understood, it could mean a previously badly defined argument or account that is said to hold good. The Greek here does not name that referent or establish the speaker’s identity. “Wrongly defined” preserves κακῶς with προδιωρισμένον rather than changing it to “defined as evil.” The earlier concern was whether an intelligible grammatical construction could be supported at all; the implied-subject genitive-absolute analysis supplies one. The remaining referent and attachment uncertainty is disclosed rather than resolved by invention, so it is not treated here as an unreadable-source or missing-clause block. This remains a candidate interpretation requiring independent review.

The selected edition has two dots, accent marks, and a third dot after “custom.” The three dots and intervening marks are retained exactly as a printed gap; no conjunction or missing argument is supplied.

The square brackets mark supplied letters within words, not a dot-count lacuna. The supplied Greek is translated as printed (“forbidden as something most grievous”), and no additional conjectural letters are supplied.

source_issues.source_quote: κἂν οὖν ἑνὸς οὐδήποτε ὁμολογουμένου εἶναι ἁμαρτήματα
source_issues.issue: The construction is compressed: ἑνός is singular, while ἁμαρτήματα is plural, and οὐδήποτε is unusual in this position. “In any one case it is acknowledged that there are sins” takes ἑνός as one acknowledged instance and retains the plural sins. An alternative is “even if a single person anywhere acknowledges that there are sins.” The conclusion does not require specifying which referent of ἑνός is intended.

passages.text:
Peter said, “We remember that our Lord and teacher gave us this command: ‘Keep the mysteries for me and for the sons of my house.’ That is also why ‘he explained to his own disciples in private’ the mysteries of the kingdom of the heavens. But to tell the secret things to you, who fight against us and scrutinize nothing other than what is ours .... (whether true or false), is to act impiously. Yet, so that some of those standing here may not suppose that I am devising a pretext because I am unable to answer what you have said, I will speak, first asking you: if there were no suffering pain, what would the evil one still be?”

Simon said, “Nothing.”

Peter said, “Is evil, then, suffering pain and dying?”

Simon said, “It seems so.”

Peter said, “Then evil does not always exist; indeed, it cannot have existence. For suffering pain and dying are among the things that happen, neither of which occurs when sound health is present. For what is suffering pain other than something being out of harmony? And what is death other than the separation of a soul from a body? Thus there is no suffering pain when harmony exists. For dying is not even among things that have existence at all, because death is nothing, as I said, other than the separation of a soul from a body. When this occurs, the body, being naturally without perception, dissolves, but the soul, possessing perception, exists alive. Hence, when harmony exists, there is no suffering pain, no dying; nor indeed are there deadly plants, venomous creeping creatures, or anything else of this sort whose outcome is death. Hence, when immortality prevails, it will become apparent that everything has come into being with good reason. And this will indeed be so when the human being becomes immortal because of righteousness, with the Messiah’s peaceful kingdom prevailing, when his constitution too is well-balanced, so that not sharp ........ impulses; and his knowledge is also unerring, so that he may not [π.......] any of the evils as good; and he will be in pain, so that he may not be mortal.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ μυστήρια ἐμοὶ καὶ τοῖς υἱοῖς τοῦ οἴκου μου φυλάξατε
lexical_decisions.chosen: Keep the mysteries for me and for the sons of my house
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative recipients are retained as “for,” rather than converting the phrase into an unexpressed prohibition. “Preserve” is another rendering of φυλάξατε.

lexical_decisions.chosen: of the kingdom of the heavens
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural οὐρανῶν is retained without substituting an explanatory circumlocution such as God’s rule.

ἀλγεῖν concerns pain or suffering; “no suffering pain” preserves the experiential act rather than making it identical by definition with every moral evil. The subsequent ὁ πονηρός is rendered personally as “the evil one,” while τὸ πονηρόν is the abstract “evil.”

This contrasts occurrences or events with τὰ ὑπαρκτά, things that have existence. “Accidents” has a possible technical philosophical sense but is less accessible and could mislead in ordinary English.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ αἰσθητὴ οὖσα ζῶσα ὑπάρχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: but the soul, possessing perception, exists alive
lexical_decisions.rationale: αἰσθητή normally can denote perceptible, but here it contrasts the body’s ἀναίσθητον and supports a sense of having sensation. “Being perceptible” is the lexical alternative and is preserved here rather than treated as impossible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς τοῦ χριστοῦ εἰρηνικῆς ἐπικρατούσης βασιλείας
lexical_decisions.chosen: with the Messiah’s peaceful kingdom prevailing
lexical_decisions.rationale: χριστοῦ is an independent title, so “Messiah” follows the supplied POB policy. The possessive and the adjective peaceful are retained.
The cognate words describe a well-mixed bodily constitution. The rendering is consistent with constitution for κρᾶσις in 19.16.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν ἀθανασίας ἐπικρατούσης εὐλόγως πάντα γεγονότα φανήσεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: Hence, when immortality prevails, it will become apparent that everything has come into being with good reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes εὐλόγως (“with good reason,” “reasonably”) with γεγονότα (“having come into being”): immortality will make apparent the rationale of things that have come into being. This is supported contextually by the argument’s discussion of the usefulness and eventual suitability of created things, not uniquely established by word order. A material alternative attaches εὐλόγως to φανήσεται: “Hence, when immortality prevails, it will reasonably appear that everything has come into being.” On that reading the reasonableness concerns the appearance or inference rather than directly characterizing the rationale of coming into being. Both are grammatically available; the note preserves the alternative without asserting that the main attachment is the only possible one.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ ἡμέτερα .... (εἴτε ἀληθῆ ὄντα εἴτε ψευδῆ)
source_issues.issue: The four-dot gap after “what is ours” is preserved as exactly four dots. The source’s parenthetical true/false alternatives are retained; no missing purpose or verb is reconstructed.

The printed eight-dot gap is preserved as exactly eight dots. The surviving words are rendered as the visibly incomplete “so that not sharp ........ impulses.” No verb such as “experience,” “have,” or “feel” is invented for the missing text.

source_issues.source_quote: ἵνα μή τι τῶν κακῶν ὡς ἀγαθὸν π....... τε ἀλγῶν ἔσται, ἵνα μὴ θνητὸς ᾖ
source_issues.issue: The partial π and seven-dot gap are retained literally, with no conjectural verb. The surviving τε ἀλγῶν ἔσται is positive: “and he will be in pain.” The main text does not silently add “not” to harmonize it with surrounding claims of freedom from pain. The final “so that he may not be mortal” is retained. The loss could affect the attachment or scope of the surviving clauses; no claim is made to recover that lost syntax.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
